strengths: Natural and clearly motivated combination of MLMC with Stein-based control functionals; the resulting estimator applies to unnormalized densities and MCMC samples, which is more general than multilevel Bayesian quadrature (restricted to tractable kernel/distribution pairs).

Simple, easy-to-implement estimator with an unbiased split-sample variant and a biased simplified variant; unbiasedness is proven and a per-level variance bound is provided that inherits the O(m^{-τ/d}) rate of control functionals.

Includes a real-data Bayesian inference example (Lotka–Volterra with hare/lynx data, NUTS samples via Stan) in addition to a standard MLMC ODE test case, and examines QMC/LHS designs for the simplified estimator.
weaknesses: Very limited novelty: the method is a direct per-level application of existing control functionals to the standard MLMC telescoping sum, structurally identical to multilevel BQ (Li et al., 2023) with CF substituted for BQ. Theorem 2 is simply the sum of the Oates et al. (2019) per-level bounds and offers no new technical insight.

No cost-complexity analysis, which is the defining element of multilevel methods (cf. Giles' complexity theorem). The paper does not derive optimal sample allocation for MLCF nor show that the total cost to reach accuracy ε improves over MLMC/CF; the conclusion explicitly defers this to a 'full version', and the experiments use sample sizes optimal for MLMC rather than MLCF.

Weak and incomplete empirical evaluation: only two low-dimensional problems with 3 levels; finest-level sample sizes of 2–6 make fitting a kernel control functional essentially degenerate (with the simplified estimator and n=2 the level estimate is nearly a weighted mean of two points); results shown only as small box plots without numerical tables; no ablation on kernel/lengthscale choice or the m/n split.

Missing relevant baseline: multilevel Bayesian quadrature is feasible on the Gaussian-input ODE example (SE kernel + Gaussian is a tractable pair) yet is not compared, despite the paper claiming the competing methods are 'very difficult or not feasible'.

Theoretical assumptions (compact hypercube domain, boundary vanishing, functions in the Stein RKHS, fill-distance conditions) are acknowledged to be violated in both experiments, so the theory does not actually cover the presented results; A4 is oddly stated ('for all distributions Π′').

Practical costs are not discussed: O(m^3) kernel solves, the need for ∇log π (which for the ODE posterior requires ODE sensitivities), and hyperparameter tuning are not accounted for in the budget, and it is unclear whether the reported budget includes CF fitting time.

Reproducibility is limited: no code, no kernel hyperparameter details, no description of the reparameterisation, priors, MCMC settings, or how the reference 'true' integral was obtained for computing absolute error.

Presentation issues: numerous typos ('Baysian', 'simply the equations', 'multilevel control function'), notational errors in Proposition 1 (f_{l−1}(x_{(l−1,i)}) should be x_{(l,i)}; index starting at i=0), duplicated 'l = 1' column headers in Tables 1–2, and a very short main text that reads as a preliminary/workshop report.
